claims.text: A random elemental distribution in multi-component concentrated alloys causes severe lattice distortion.
Significant atomic-size mismatch contributes to severe lattice distortion.
Severe lattice distortion alters dislocation-core structure.
Severe random lattice distortion forces edge-dislocation cores away from their neutral planes into wavy, non-planar paths.
Wavy, non-planar dislocation configurations increase the energy barrier for glide and reduce dislocation mobility.
Reduced dislocation mobility caused by lattice distortion increases yield strength.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism modifies work hardening and ductility.
NbTaTiV is a refractory high-entropy alloy that can exist as a single BCC solid solution.
The initial NbTaTiV-like BCC solid solution has a high degree of chemical randomness and associated lattice distortion.
Rapid quenching from homogenization preserves a random elemental arrangement and maximizes lattice distortion.
Prolonged high-temperature annealing promotes local chemical ordering.
Prolonged high-temperature annealing relaxes lattice strain and reduces lattice distortion.
The quenched, more random alloy will have higher yield strength than the annealed, locally ordered alloy.
The quenched alloy will exhibit wavy, non-planar dislocation cores, whereas the annealed alloy will permit more planar glide.
Differences in lattice distortion between the two processing states will produce distinguishable work-hardening behavior and dislocation mobility.
The mechanism is expected to operate from room temperature to approximately 900 °C.
The hypothesis applies principally to BCC or similar concentrated alloys with significant atomic-size mismatch when precipitation and grain-boundary strengthening are minimized or held constant.
Local chemical ordering may overlap with or confound the effects attributed to lattice distortion.
